```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
```

> **In this step** we fit one linear mixed model per probe and split each
> probe's expression variance into parts explained by cell type, donor, age,
> sex, batch and noise. We fit three models: one using both cell types
> together, and one within each cell type.
>
> **Reads:** `data/processed/immvar.rds` (from Step 1)<br>
> **Writes:** `results/models/{combined,CD4_T,Monocyte}.rds` and matching CSV
> tables in `results/tables/`<br>
> **Run time:** a few seconds when saved fits exist. Fitting from scratch takes
> about 30 minutes on one CPU core, or about 5 minutes on eight; see
> [Fit every probe](#fit-every-probe).

# What variancePartition does

Expression of a gene varies from one array to the next. Some of that variation
is explained by things we recorded, such as which cell type was measured or
which donor it came from, and the rest is noise. **variancePartition** fits a
**linear mixed model** to each probe and divides the total variance into one
piece per variable:

```
total variance = cell type + donor + sex + batch + age + residual
```

Each piece is then divided by the total to give a **variance fraction**. The
fractions for a probe are between 0 and 1 and **always add up to 1 (100%)**.
For example, if cell type has a fraction of 0.80 for a probe, then 80% of that
probe's variation across arrays is associated with cell type.

## The terms in our model

| Term | How it enters the model | What it captures |
|---|---|---|
| `CellType` | random effect `(1 | CellType)` | Differences between naïve CD4 T cells and monocytes |
| `Individual` | random effect `(1 | Individual)` | Differences between **donors** that persist across their arrays |
| `Sex` | random effect `(1 | Sex)` | Differences between female and male donors |
| `Batch` | random effect `(1 | Batch)` | Technical differences between processing batches |
| `Age` | fixed effect `Age` | A straight-line trend with age |
| `Residuals` | — | Everything else: measurement noise and unrecorded factors |

**Why are categorical variables random effects?** The variancePartition authors
recommend modelling categorical variables as random effects, written
`(1 | variable)`, and continuous variables such as age as fixed effects. For
variables with only a few categories, such as sex or cell type, the choice
makes little difference. For variables with many categories, such as the
hundreds of donors here, a random effect is needed to obtain correct variance
estimates. Step 4 checks this by refitting with sex and cell type as fixed
effects.

**What does the donor term mean?** In the combined model, the donor effect is
shared by a person's T-cell and monocyte arrays, so it captures person-level
differences that appear in **both** cell types. Genetics is one such
difference, but the donor fraction is **not** a heritability estimate.

# Setup

```{r packages}
.libPaths(c("library", .libPaths()))
library(variancePartition)  # fitExtractVarPartModel(), calcVarPart()
library(BiocParallel)       # SerialParam() / MulticoreParam(): run fits in parallel
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Load the prepared data

We keep only the analysis cohort (the `included` arrays from Step 1). Age is
**standardised** to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. This helps the model
fitting numerically and does not change Age's variance fraction.

```{r load-data}
data <- readRDS("data/processed/immvar.rds")

expression <- data$expression[, data$metadata$included]
metadata   <- droplevels(data$metadata[data$metadata$included, ])
metadata$Age <- as.numeric(scale(metadata$Age))

# Arrays (columns) and metadata rows must be in the same order.
stopifnot(identical(colnames(expression), rownames(metadata)))
dir.create("results/models", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

c(probes  = nrow(expression),
  arrays  = ncol(expression),
  donors  = nlevels(metadata$Individual),
  batches = nlevels(metadata$Batch))
```

# The model formulas

The formulas have no left-hand side because variancePartition applies them to
**every row** of the expression matrix in turn.

```{r formulas}
# Both cell types together
combined_formula <- ~ Age + (1 | Sex) + (1 | CellType) + (1 | Batch) + (1 | Individual)

# One cell type at a time, so there is no cell type term
within_formula <- ~ Age + (1 | Sex) + (1 | Batch) + (1 | Individual)
```

**A caution about the within-cell models.** Inside a single cell type, most
donors have just one array. Only donors with **repeat arrays** let the model
tell "this person differs from others" apart from random noise. The donor
fractions from the within-cell models therefore rest on a small number of
repeats and should be interpreted cautiously.

# Walkthrough: one probe, by hand {#walkthrough}

Before fitting more than 21,000 probes, let us open the black box for a single
probe. We use **TLR4** (probe `8157524`), a receptor that monocytes express and
naïve T cells do not.

```{r one-probe-plot, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3}
probe <- "8157524"  # TLR4

one_probe <- metadata
one_probe$expression <- expression[probe, ]

ggplot(one_probe, aes(CellType, expression)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log2 expression", title = "TLR4 expression by cell type") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The two cell types barely overlap, so we expect cell type to explain most of
this probe's variance. We fit the same mixed model directly with `lme4`, the
package variancePartition uses internally:

```{r one-probe-fit}
fit <- lme4::lmer(
  expression ~ Age + (1 | Sex) + (1 | CellType) + (1 | Batch) + (1 | Individual),
  data = one_probe,
  REML = FALSE
)
```

Next we collect the variance pieces:

1. **Random effects and residual.** `VarCorr()` reports these directly, in the
   `vcov` column.
2. **Age.** This is a fixed effect, so its piece is the variance of
   Age's contribution (Age × its slope) across the arrays.

```{r one-probe-pieces}
random_parts <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(fit))
random_parts[, c("grp", "vcov")]

age_contribution <- one_probe$Age * lme4::fixef(fit)[["Age"]]
age_part <- mean((age_contribution - mean(age_contribution))^2)

pieces <- c(setNames(random_parts$vcov, random_parts$grp), Age = age_part)
names(pieces)[names(pieces) == "Residual"] <- "Residuals"
```

Divide each piece by the total and compare the result with variancePartition.
`calcVarPart()` computes fractions from a fitted model, and
`fitExtractVarPartModel()` fits **and** computes in one call. This is the
function we use for all probes below.

```{r one-probe-compare}
by_hand <- pieces / sum(pieces)

from_calcVarPart <- calcVarPart(fit)

# fitExtractVarPartModel() expects several probes (it fails on a single row),
# so we give it our three example probes and keep the TLR4 row.
example_probes <- c("8157524", "8177232", "7903765")  # TLR4, KDM5D, GSTM1
from_fitExtract <- fitExtractVarPartModel(
  expression[example_probes, ], combined_formula, metadata,
  REML = FALSE, useInitialFit = FALSE, BPPARAM = SerialParam()
)

components <- names(from_calcVarPart)
data.frame(
  component              = components,
  by_hand                = signif(by_hand[components], 4),
  calcVarPart            = signif(from_calcVarPart[components], 4),
  fitExtractVarPartModel = signif(unlist(from_fitExtract[probe, components]), 4),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

All three columns agree, and each adds up to 1. For TLR4, cell type explains
about **`r round(100 * by_hand[["CellType"]])`%** of the variance. That is all
variancePartition does for each probe: fit a mixed model, then express each
variance component as a share of the total.

> **Note:** for some probes, lme4 reports a *"boundary (singular) fit"*. That
> means one variance was estimated as exactly zero (often batch, here). It is
> expected and is not an error.

# Fit every probe {#fit-every-probe}

`fitExtractVarPartModel()` repeats the walkthrough for every row of the
expression matrix. We use two settings deliberately:

* `REML = FALSE` fits by maximum likelihood, the variancePartition default. We
  set it explicitly so the choice is visible.
* `useInitialFit = FALSE` fits each probe from scratch. By default the package
  fits the first probe and uses its solution as the starting point for all the
  others. That is faster, but a starting point at a boundary, such as a
  variance of exactly zero, can then carry over to probes where it does not
  belong.

The helper below fits one model, checks the output and saves it:

```{r fit-function}
fit_and_save <- function(expression, metadata, formula, name, backend) {
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(expression), rownames(metadata)))
  message("Fitting ", name, ": ", nrow(expression), " probes, ",
          ncol(expression), " arrays")

  result <- fitExtractVarPartModel(expression, formula, metadata,
                                   REML = FALSE, useInitialFit = FALSE,
                                   BPPARAM = backend)
  result <- as.data.frame(result)

  # Every probe must be present, and its fractions must be valid and sum to 1.
  stopifnot(identical(rownames(result), rownames(expression)),
            all(is.finite(as.matrix(result))),
            all(as.matrix(result) >= 0),
            max(abs(rowSums(result) - 1)) < 1e-6)

  saveRDS(result, paste0("results/models/", name, ".rds"))
  fwrite(data.frame(probe_id = rownames(result), result),
         paste0("results/tables/", name, ".csv"))
  message("Finished ", name)
}
```

**Saving time.** Fitting three models to more than 21,000 probes each is the
slow part of this project. The next chunk therefore **reuses saved results**
whenever `results/models/<name>.rds` already exists. To force a fresh fit, knit
with the parameter `refit: true`. In RStudio, use *Knit ▸ Knit with
Parameters…*. To use several CPU cores, set `workers` to more than 1. The
results are the same; only the speed changes.

```{r fit-or-load-function}
backend <- if (params$workers > 1) {
  MulticoreParam(workers = params$workers)  # on Windows, use SnowParam() instead
} else {
  SerialParam()
}

fit_or_load <- function(expression, metadata, formula, name) {
  saved_file <- paste0("results/models/", name, ".rds")
  if (params$refit || !file.exists(saved_file)) {
    started <- Sys.time()
    fit_and_save(expression, metadata, formula, name, backend)
    action <- sprintf("fitted now (%.1f minutes)",
                      as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), started, units = "mins")))
  } else {
    action <- "loaded saved results"
  }
  data.frame(model = name, arrays = ncol(expression), status = action)
}
```

```{r fit-models, message = TRUE}
is_t_cell   <- metadata$CellType == "CD4_T"
is_monocyte <- metadata$CellType == "Monocyte"

rbind(
  fit_or_load(expression, metadata, combined_formula, "combined"),
  fit_or_load(expression[, is_t_cell],   droplevels(metadata[is_t_cell, ]),
              within_formula, "CD4_T"),
  fit_or_load(expression[, is_monocyte], droplevels(metadata[is_monocyte, ]),
              within_formula, "Monocyte")
)

capture.output(sessionInfo(), file = "results/sessionInfo.txt")
```

# A first look at the results

Each result is a table with **one row per probe** and **one column per variance
component**:

```{r first-look}
combined <- readRDS("results/models/combined.rds")

dim(combined)
head(round(combined, 3))

range(rowSums(combined))  # every row adds up to 1
```

The TLR4 row from the full fit matches the walkthrough above:

```{r tlr4-row}
round(combined[probe, ], 4)
```

# Summary

* We fitted **three models** to
  **`r format(nrow(expression), big.mark = ",")` probes**: the combined model
  (`r ncol(expression)` arrays) and one within each cell type.
* Each probe now has six variance fractions that add up to 1.
* The walkthrough showed exactly how a fraction is calculated, and that our
  by-hand numbers match variancePartition.
